DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS FOLLOWING LEG BYPASS SURGERY

This information is designed as a guideline to assist you in a
speedy recovery from your surgery. Please follow these
guidelines unless your physician has specifically instructed you
otherwise. Please call our office nurse if you have any
questions. Dial 911 if you have any medical emergency.

ACTIVITY:

There are no specific restrictions on activity. You should be as
active as is comfortable. Some fatigue is expected for the first
several weeks. Leg swelling is typical following this type of
surgery and can be controlled by elevating your leg above the
level of your heart when you are not walking.

PLEASE CALL US IMMEDIATELY FOR ANY OF THE FOLLOWING PROBLEMS:

Redness in or drainage from your leg wound(s).

New pain, numbness or discoloration of your foot or toes.

Watch for signs and symptoms of infection. These are: a fever
greater than 101 degrees, chills, increased redness, or pus
draining from the incision site. If you experience any of these
or bleeding at the incision site, CALL THE DOCTOR.

Exercise:

Limit strenuous activity for 4 weeks.

No heavy lifting greater than 20 pounds for the next 7 days.

No Driving.

BATHING/SHOWERING:

You shower immediately upon coming home. No bathing. A clear
dressing may cover your leg incision and this should be left in
place for three (3) days. Remove it after this time and wash
your incision(s) gently with soap and water. Dissolving sutures,
which do not have to be removed, were probably used.

If you have staples these will be removed on your follow-up
appointment.

WOUND CARE:

Sutures / Staples may be removed before discharge. If they are
not, an appointment will be made for you to return for removal.

When the sutures / staples are removed the doctor may or may not
place pieces of tape called steri-strips over the incision.
These will stay on about a week and you may shower with them on.
If these do not fall off after 10 days, you may peel them off
with warm water and soap in the shower.

Avoid taking a tub bath, swimming, or soaking in a hot tub for
two weeks after surgery.

MEDICATIONS:

Unless told otherwise you should resume taking all of the
medications you were taking before surgery. You will be given a
new prescription for pain medication, which can be taken every
three (3) to four (4) hours only if necessary.

Remember that narcotic pain meds can be constipating and you
should increase the fluid and bulk foods in your diet. (Check
with your physician if you have fluid restrictions.) If you feel
that you are constipated, do not strain at the toilet. You may
use over the counter Metamucil or Milk of Magnesia. Appetite
suppression may occur; this will improve with time. Eat small
balanced meals throughout the day.

CAUTIONS:

NO SMOKING! We know you've heard this before, but it really is
an important step to your recovery. Smoking causes narrowing of
your blood vessels which in turn decreases circulation. If you
smoke you will need to stop as soon as possible. Ask your nurse
or doctor for information on smoking cessation.

Avoid bending for 4-6 weeks.

No strenuous activity for 4-6 weeks after surgery.

DIET :

There are no special restrictions on your diet postoperatively.
Poor appetite is expected for several weeks and small, frequent
meals may be preferred.

For people with [**Location (un) 1106**] problems we would recommend a
cholesterol lowering diet: Follow a diet low in total fat and
low in saturated fat and in cholesterol to improve lipid profile
in your blood. Additionally, some people see a reduction in
serum cholesterol by reducing dietary cholesterol. Since a
reduction in dietary cholesterol is not harmful, we suggest that
most people reduce dietary fat, saturated fat and cholesterol to
decrease total cholesterol and LDL (Low Density Lipoprotein-the
bad cholesterol). Exercise will increase your HDL (High Density
Lipoprotein-the good cholesterol) and with your doctor's
permission, is typically recommended. You may be self-referred
or get a referral from your doctor.

If you are overweight, you need to think about starting a weight
management program. Your health and its improvement depend on
it. We know that making changes in your lifestyle will not be
easy, and it will require a whole new set of habits and a new
attitude. If interested you can may be self-referred or can get
a referral from your doctor.

If you have diabetes and would like additional guidance, you may
request a referral from your doctor.

FOLLOW-UP APPOINTMENT:

Be sure to keep your medical appointments. The key to your
improving health will be to keep a tight reign on any of the
chronic medical conditions that you have. Things like high blood
pressure, diabetes, and high cholesterol are major villains to
the blood vessels. Don't let them go untreated!

Please call the office on the first working day after your
discharge from the hospital to schedule a follow-up visit. This
should be scheduled on the calendar for seven to fourteen days
after discharge. Normal office hours are 8:30-5:00 Monday
through Friday.

PLEASE FEEL FREE TO CALL THE OFFICE WITH ANY OTHER CONCERNS OR
QUESTIONS THAT MIGHT ARISE.

This is an 80 yof with hx of diastolic CHF with 4+TR, OSA, COPD,
   Pulmonary HTN on 5L home oxygen, sinus arrest s/p PCM placement who
   initially presented to the hospital with hypoxia and worsening
   bilateral lower extremity swelling and redness.
   In the ED, initial vs were: T 98 P 60 BP 145/58 R 20 100% on NRB O2
   sat. CXR was significant for volume overload and pt was given Lasix
   80mg IV with some improvement in symptoms. Pt was offered bipap but
   refused. She was also given IV Vancomycin for presumed lower extremity
   cellulitis.
   On the medical floor she was initially diuresed with improved
   saturations.  today the patient was found to be somnolent in her room,
   with O2 desaturation into the 70s.  She was placed on NRB initially,
   Lasix 80mg x 1,  and given a nebulizer treatment with improvement in O2
   sat to 91%.  ABG done which showed 7.32/72/46.  She was transferred to
   the MICU for BIPAP and further care.
   On arrival to the MICU, patient had an O2 sat of 90% but somnolent.
   She did awaken when moved from gurney to bed.
   Hypoxemia
   Assessment:
   Pt. exhibits crackles in bases, diminished throughout. Pt. has been
   refusing BiPAP/ facemasks on day shift, recived on NC 5L, sat 88-89%,
   goal sat 89-91.
   Action:
   Allowed patient to sit on side of bed, resting on pillow on bedside
   table. While lying in the bed pt desat to 80%, placed on cool neb abd
   refused for  BPAP.
   Response:
   Sat 81-94%.  NC 5L pt desat to 80, refused to go back on cool neb.
   Plan:
   Continue to diuresis pt,  As desired by Cardiology notes, goal SAT no
   higher then 91%.BPAP as tolerates
   Impaired Skin Integrity
   Assessment:
   Pt. venous stasis changes on her bilateral lower legs. They are
   erythemic and edematous.  Not considered to be cellulitis as redness is
   bilateral.
   Action:
   Legs elevated as able, compression boots placed, but pt refused
   Response:
   Patient can be difficult regarding wearing equipment , at times becomes
   combative striking and screaming at staff.
   Plan:
   Monitor area for skin breakdown.

This is an 80 yo f with hx of diastolic CHF with 4+TR, OSA, COPD,
   Pulmonary HTN on 5L home oxygen, sinus arrest s/p PCM placement who
   initially presented to the hospital with hypoxia and worsening
   bilateral lower extremity swelling and redness.
   In the ED, initial vs were: T 98 P 60 BP 145/58 R 20 100% on NRB O2
   sat. CXR was significant for volume overload and pt was given Lasix
   80mg IV with some improvement in symptoms. Pt was offered bipap but
   refused. She was also given IV Vancomycin for presumed lower extremity
   cellulitis.
   On the medical floor she was initially diuresed with improved
   saturations.  Today the patient was found to be somnolent in her room,
   with O2 desaturation into the 70s.  She was placed on NRB initially,
   Lasix 80mg x 1, and given a nebulizer treatment with improvement in O2
   sat to 91%.  ABG was done which showed 7.32/72/46.  She was transferred
   to the MICU for BIPAP and further care.
   On arrival to the MICU, patient had an O2 sat of 90% but somnolent.
   She did awaken when moved from gurney to bed.
   Hypoxemia
   Assessment:
   Pt. exhibits crackles in bases, diminished throughout. Pt. has been
   refusing BiPAP/ facemasks. Remained on NC 5L, SAT 85-93%, goal sat
   89-91. DeSAT
s to 75 when she removes her nasal cannula. With Russian
   interpreter, patient is alert and oriented x3.
   Action:
   Patient either dangles legs on side of bed leaning on table, or lies on
   R side in bed.  OOB to commode with 1 assist. Becomes short of breath
   with any activity. Diuretics changed from IV to PO.
   Response:
   Maintaining SAT 84-93% on 5 L O2. Per patient via interpreter, patient
   states breathing feels more comfortable today.  Slept much of shift,
   easily aroused to voice.
   Plan:
   Continue to diuresis pt.  As desired by Cardiology notes, goal SAT no
   higher then 91%. BPAP at night if patient agrees to it.  Potential call
   out to floor tomorrow if tolerating new PO diuretic regimen.
   Impaired Skin Integrity
   Assessment:
   Pt. has venous stasis changes on her bilateral lower legs. They are
   erythemic and edematous.  Not considered to be cellulitis as redness is
   bilateral. Patient states her legs always look this way.
   Action:
   Legs elevated as able, compression boots placed, but pt refused to
   allow nurse to attach them to machine and turn on.
   Response:
   Patient can be difficult regarding wearing equipment , at times becomes
   combative striking and screaming at staff.
   Plan:
   Monitor area for skin breakdown.

This is an 80 yo f with hx of diastolic CHF with 4+TR, OSA, COPD,
   Pulmonary HTN on 5L home oxygen, sinus arrest s/p PCM placement who
   initially presented to the hospital with hypoxia and worsening
   bilateral lower extremity swelling and redness.
   In the ED, initial vs were: T 98 P 60 BP 145/58 R 20 100% on NRB O2
   sat. CXR was significant for volume overload and pt was given Lasix
   80mg IV with some improvement in symptoms. Pt was offered bipap but
   refused. She was also given IV Vancomycin for presumed lower extremity
   cellulitis.
   On the medical floor she was initially diuresed with improved
   saturations.  Today the patient was found to be somnolent in her room,
   with O2 desaturation into the 70s.  She was placed on NRB initially,
   Lasix 80mg x 1, and given a nebulizer treatment with improvement in O2
   sat to 91%.  ABG was done which showed 7.32/72/46.  She was transferred
   to the MICU for BIPAP and further care.
   On arrival to the MICU, patient had an O2 sat of 90% but somnolent.
   She did awaken when moved from gurney to bed.
   Hypoxemia
   Assessment:
   Pt. exhibits crackles in bases, diminished throughout. Pt. looks
   depressed, but alert/oriented x3. Remained on NC 5L, SAT 85-93%, goal
   sat 89-91.
   Action:
   Patient either dangles legs on side of bed leaning on table, or lies on
   R side in bed.  OOB to commode with 1 assist. Becomes short of breath
   with any activity. Pt tolerates BiPAP fro 3hr
   Response:
   Maintaining SAT 84-93% on 5 L O2. patient states breathing feels more
   comfortable today.  Slept much of shift, easily aroused to voice.
   Tolerating PO diuretics.
   Plan:
   Continue to diuresis pt.  As desired by Cardiology notes, goal SAT no
   higher then 91%. BPAP at night if patient agrees to it.  Plan to
   discharge to either home with services, to rehab ( pt
s refusing to go
   to rehab), or to call out under care of Hospitalist (so patient will
   not be triggered back to unit).
   Impaired Skin Integrity
   Assessment:
   Pt. has venous stasis changes on her bilateral lower legs. They are
   erythemic and edematous.  Not considered to be cellulitis as redness is
   bilateral. Patient states her legs always look this way.
   Action:
   Legs elevated as able, refuses compression boots.
   Response:
   Patient can be difficult regarding wearing equipment, at times becomes
   combative.

HOSPITAL COURSE BY SYSTEM:

1.  ENDOCRINE:  The patient presented to the [**Hospital1 346**] Emergency Department with a serum
glucose of 407, an anion gap of at least 26, dry mucous
membranes, severe acidemia, glucosuria, and ketonuria; all of
which were consistent with a presentation of diabetic
ketoacidosis.

respirations tachypnea that quickly began to improve as her
acidemia improved.  She was administered a bolus of 10 units
of regular insulin intravenously while in the Emergency
Department, and she was then started on an insulin drip at

aggressively resuscitated with intravenous fluids; initially

euglycemia throughout the remainder of the hospitalization.

sliding-scale during the day and 30 units of insulin Glargine

hospitalization.  Although, it was less than 5 on admission,

presentation with diabetic ketoacidosis, she subsequently
manifested many of the electrolyte abnormalities consistent
with this diagnosis.  Of note, she developed severe
hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and
hypophosphatemia.  All of these electrolytes were
aggressively repleted throughout the course of her
hospitalization.

the time of her discharge.

3.  CARDIOVASCULAR:   The patient's initial tachycardia and
relative hypotension improved following her extensive fluid
resuscitation.  Overall, she was roughly 10 liters to 11
liters positive throughout this hospitalization.

4.  GASTROINTESTINAL:  Although there was an initial concern
for an acute surgical abdomen, diabetic ketoacidosis can
often present with abdominal pain that mimics a surgical
abdomen.  Although the possibilities of acute cholecystitis
and acute appendicitis were ruled out with the appropriate
imaging studies.  The patient's abdominal pain spontaneously
resolved by hospital day two.  She had no subsequent nausea,
vomiting, or diarrhea.

5.  INFECTIOUS DISEASE:  While the patient had a significant
leukocytosis on presentation, this was also likely secondary
to her presentation with diabetic ketoacidosis.  Her
leukocytosis spontaneously resolved with resolution of her
diabetic ketoacidosis, and she had no longer had a
leukocytosis at the time of discharge.

6.  SUMMARY:  Overall, at the time of discharge, the patient
was tolerating a regular diabetic diet.  She was back on her
baseline insulin regimen, and all of her laboratory
abnormalities present on admission had resolved.  She was
therefore deemed stable for discharge to home with close
followup by her primary endocrinologist.

DISCHARGE STATUS:  The patient was discharged to home.

vancomycin for 14 days and Imipenum ongoing. Improvement of
respiratory status.
.
# MRSA Bacteremia - Most likely from pulmonary source from HAP.
Treated with 14 day course of vancomycin.  TTE without
vegetations. Surveillance cultures negative.
.
# Asthma - Patient with severe wheezing on exam improved with
steroids and aggressive nebs for asthma.  She was treated with
solumedrol then transitioned to prednisone for long taper of
steroids. We increased here advair dose to 500/50.  She was
treated with standing xopenex (instead of albuterol because of
tachycardia) and ipratropium nebs with albuterol prn.  She was
weaned to supplemental O2 of 2-3L with sats 93-98%.  ABG with
likely respiratory acidosis as compensation for metabolic
alkalosis.
.
# C. diff - Patient tested + for c.diff toxin.  She will need to
continue IV flagyl for 7-14 days after completion of imipenum.
.
# Tachycardia - Appears sinus vs MAT.  Patient had tachycardia
in the 100s which improvd to 90's on 25mg TID of betablocker.
Monitor closely for bronchospasm in setting of steroid taper.
Could consider change to diltiazem.
.
# Metabolic Alkalosis - Urine cl of 110, thus likely secondary
to steroids.  [**Month (only) 116**] have component of respiratory acidosis from
pulm disease although pulm is more likely compensatory.
.
# DM - Patient had DM type 2 on admission.  Concern about
progression of pancreatitis with possible insufficient insulin
production.  Would treat like DM1 in terms of needing some basal
insulin if NPO.  Treated with insulin gtt while on high dose
steroids and transitioned to glargine and humalog ISS.  Patient
had decreasing insulin needs with steroid taper.  She was
discharged on a significantly lower dose of glargine than she
had been on 22 to 12U to avoid hypoglycemia.  Patient did have
several early morning low sugars (50-60s) which easily responded
to PO intake.  Dosing was changed from noon to in the morning,
which appeared to help.
.
# Hyperlipidemia - Hold PO lipitor in setting of likely steroid
induced myopathy.
.
# HTN - Normotensive. Tolerated Beta blocker.
.
# Depression/Anxiety - Patient with situational depression and
passive suicidal ideation.  Psychiatry was consulted.  She was
started on Remeron QHS to help with depression, sleep and
appetite with good effect.  She was tappered off of ativan and
started on standing 12.5 mg TID of seroquel (25mg TID made her
very sleepy).  Her preferences are no morphine (causes
hallucinations) and no sedating medications during the day.
Palliative care and social work were involved.
.
# Malnutrition - Likely secondary to prolonged hospitalization
and frequent periods of NPO as well as concurrent infection
(pneumonia, bacteremia, c.diff, pancreatitis).
She was started on pancreatic enzymes to help with digestion and
absorption.  She was taking good POs with supplements TID at
discharge.

# Right venous thrombosis - secondary to PICC line.  We removed
the right PICC line and placed a smaller single lumen PICC in
the left arm.  Based on the risk benefit of systemic
anticoagulation and repeat GIB the decision was made to hold on
anticoagulation.  Repeat ultrasound showed resolution.
.
# Pressure ulcer - admitted with pressure ulcer.  Wound care was
consulted with recs included.
.

have written goals of care.  Signed form to go with patient.

   required frequent suctioning of the mouth. NTS x1 by respirartory
   therapy for fair amounts of thin, white secretions. Occational
   exertional wheezing treated with albuterol/atrovent nebs x2 this
   afternoon.
   Action:
   Extubated without significant agitation although he appears to be
   profoundly weak and deconditioned.
   Response:
   Pt tolerating transition to cool neb with an adequate repeat abg post
   extubation. Unclear whether pt will eventually fatigue and require
   reintubation. He remains npo although receiving meds via ngt.
   Plan:
   Monitor lung exam /respiratory status closely for evidence of fatigue,
   desaturation. Pt may require reintubation; keep npo.
   Altered mental status (not Delirium)
   Assessment:
   Pt is alert and oriented to place and person. Voice is garbled but
   intelligible. In addition to stating that he feels sob, he is also c/o
   [**7-27**] abdominal pain. The abdominal pain appears likely r/t
   constipation. He is passing flatus.
   Action:
   Pt is alert, generally oriented, and calm s/p extubation. Pt did
   receive a single dose of zyprexa following extubation. Receiving
   lactulose for his abdominal pain.
   Response:
   Calm s/p ?zyprexa.
   Plan:
   Monitor mental status/orientation closely. Reorient as needed, offer
   clonidine or zyprexa for anxiety.

DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS FOLLOWING AORTIC SURGERY

.

This information is designed as a guideline to assist you in a
speedy recovery from your surgery. Please follow these
guidelines unless your physician has specifically instructed you
otherwise. Please call our office nurse if you have any
questions. Dial 911 if you have any medical emergency.

.

ACTIVITY:

.

There are no specific restrictions on activity other than no
lifting an object heavier than twenty-five (25) pounds for the
first three (3) months. Gradually increase your level of
activity back to normal depending on how you feel. Fatigue is
normal, especially for the first month postoperative. Resume
driving when you feel strong enough and comfortable enough
without needing pain medication.

.

PLEASE CALL US IMMEDIATELY FOR ANY OF THE FOLLOWING PROBLEMS:

.

Severe and worsening abdominal pain .

.

Pain or swelling in one of your legs.

.

Increasing pain, redness or drainage related to your incision(s)
.

.

Watch for signs and symptoms of infection. These are: a fever
greater than 101 degrees, chills, increased redness, or pus
draining from the incision site. If you experience any of these
or bleeding at the incision site, CALL THE DOCTOR.

.

Exercise:

.

Limit strenuous activity for 8 weeks.

.

Resume driving when you feel strong enough and comfortable
enough without needing pain medication .

.

No heavy lifting greater than 20 pounds for 8 weeks.

.

Avoid excessive bending at the hips and stooping for 4 weeks.

.

BATHING/SHOWERING:

.

You may shower immediately if the incision is dry upon coming
home. No baths until sutures / staples are removed. Dissolving
sutures may have been used. In either case, you can wash your
incision gently with soap and water.

.

WOUND CARE:

.

Suture / Staples may be removed before discharge. If they are
not, an appointment will be made for you to return for staple
removal.

.

When the sutures / staples are removed the doctor may or may not
place pieces of tape called steri-strips over the incision.
These will stay on about a week and you may shower with them on.
If these do not fall off after 10 days, you may peel them off
with warm water and soap in the shower.

.

Avoid taking a tub bath, swimming, or soaking in a hot tub for
two weeks after surgery.

.

MEDICATIONS:

.

You may resume taking medication you were on prior to your
surgery unless specifically instructed otherwise by your
physician [**Name9 (PRE) **] will be given a new prescription for pain
medication, which should be taken every three (3) to four (4)
hours only if necessary.

.

Remember that narcotic pain meds can be constipating and you
should increase the fluid and bulk foods in your diet. (Check
with your physician if you have fluid restrictions.) If you feel
that you are constipated, do not strain at the toilet. You may
use over the counter Metamucil or Milk of Magnesia. Appetite
suppression may occur; this will improve with time. Eat small
balanced meals throughout the day.

.

CAUTIONS:

.

NO SMOKING! We know you've heard this before, but it really is
an important step to your recovery. Smoking causes narrowing of
your blood vessels which in turn decreases circulation. If you
smoke you will need to stop as soon as possible. Ask your nurse
or doctor for information on smoking cessation.

.

Avoid heavy lifting (over 20 pounds) for 8 weeks after surgery.

.

No strenuous activity for 4-6 weeks after surgery.

.

DIET:

.

There are no special restrictions on your diet postoperatively.
Poor appetite is expected for several weeks and small, frequent
meals may be preferred.

.

For people with vascular problems we would recommend a
cholesterol lowering diet: Follow a diet low in total fat and
low in saturated fat and in cholesterol to improve lipid profile
in your blood. Additionally, some people see a reduction in
serum cholesterol by reducing dietary cholesterol. Since a
reduction in dietary cholesterol is not harmful, we suggest that
most people reduce dietary fat, saturated fat and cholesterol to
decrease total cholesterol and LDL (Low Density Lipoprotein-the
bad cholesterol). Exercise will increase your HDL (High Density
Lipoprotein-the good cholesterol) and with your doctor's
permission, is typically recommended. You may be self-referred
or get a referral from your doctor.

.

If you are overweight, you need to think about starting a weight
management program. Your health and its improvement depend on
it. We know that making changes in your lifestyle will not be
easy, and it will require a whole new set of habits and a new
attitude. If interested you can may be self-referred or can get
a referral from your doctor.

.

If you have diabetes and would like additional guidance, you may
request a referral from your doctor.

.

FOLLOW-UP APPOINTMENT:

.

Be sure to keep your medical appointments. The key to your
improving health will be to keep a tight reign on any of the
chronic medical conditions that you have. Things like high blood
pressure, diabetes, and high cholesterol are major villains to
the blood vessels. Don't let them go untreated!

.

Please call the office on the first working day after your
discharge from the hospital to schedule a follow-up visit. This
should be scheduled on the calendar for seven to fourteen days
after discharge. Normal office hours are 8:30-5:30 Monday
through Friday.

.

PLEASE FEEL FREE TO CALL THE OFFICE WITH ANY OTHER CONCERNS OR
QUESTIONS THAT MIGHT ARISE.

Admission Date:  [**2195-8-27**]       Discharge Date:  [**2195-9-1**]


Service:  D FIRM TRANSFERRED TO CCU

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:  The patient is an 85-year-old
male, with past medical history significant for coronary
artery disease, status post three-vessel CABG, history of MI,
and type 2 diabetes, who presented to an outside hospital
with bright red blood per rectum, and transferred to [**Hospital1 18**]
for colonoscopy and further GI work-up.

The patient originally presented to [**Hospital3 22439**] on
[**8-23**], complaining of bright red blood per rectum, and
abdominal pain.  The patient was hemodynamically stable upon
admission with an hematocrit of 34.  He initially had an NG
lavage which was negative for any active bleeding.  The
patient was closely monitored with serial hematocrits.  He
had additional episodes of GI bleeding on [**8-26**] and
[**8-27**].  His crit dropped from 34 to 30.  He received
multiple blood transfusions with a total of 6 units of blood
transfused.  With these episodes of bleeding, the patient
remained hemodynamically stable and asymptomatic except for some
epigastric pressure attributed to dyspepsia.  Evaluation for
cardiac ischemia was negative. The patient was then transferred
to [**Hospital1 18**] on [**8-28**] for further GI work-up and planned
colonoscopy.  At time of arrival to [**Hospital1 18**], the patient denied any
active complaints.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS:  Positive for GI bleeding, as above.  He
denied any chest pain, shortness of breath, nausea, abdominal
pain, dizziness, or other complaints.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
1. Coronary artery disease, three-vessel CABG in [**2175**],
myocardial infarction in [**2174**] and [**2175**].
2. Diabetes mellitus type 2.
3. History of GI bleed in [**2187**] due to diverticulosis.
4. Appendectomy.

SOCIAL HISTORY:  History of tobacco abuse, quit in [**2174**].
Occasional alcohol use, approximately 1 drink per month.

MEDICATIONS AT HOME:
1. Aspirin.
2. Procardia.
3. Vioxx.
4. Inderal.
5. Isordil.
6. Zocor.
7. K-Dur.
8. Glucophage.

MEDICATIONS ON TRANSFER:
1. Glucophage 1,000 mg [**Hospital1 **].
2. Isosorbide mononitrate 30 mg qd.
3. Prilosec 20 mg [**Hospital1 **].
4. Propranolol 40 mg qid.
5. Zocor 20 mg qd.
6. Lasix 20 mg qd.
7. Procardia ER 60 mg qd.

ALLERGIES:  NKDA.

ADMISSION PHYSICAL EXAM - VITAL SIGNS:  Temperature 96.2,
blood pressure 109/58, pulse 69, respirations 18, O2 sat 97%
on room air.
GENERAL:  Patient lying in bed in no acute distress.
SKIN:  Pale.  No diaphoresis.
HEENT:  Pupils equal, round and reactive to light and
accommodation.  Extraocular movements intact.  Oropharynx
clear.
NECK:  Supple, no LAD.
CARDIOVASCULAR:  Regular rate, S1, S2, no murmurs, rubs or
gallops.
LUNGS:  Clear to auscultation and equal bilaterally.
ABDOMEN:  Soft, nontender, distended, positive bowel sounds.
EXTREMITIES:  Trace pitting edema bilaterally.

LABS AT ADMISSION:  White count 16.6, hematocrit 31.2,
platelets 232, sodium 142, K 3.7, chloride 105, bicarb 24,
BUN 19, creatinine 0.9, glucose 134.

INITIAL EKG:  Normal sinus rhythm, with a rate of 68, first
degree AV conduction delay, no ST segment changes.

HOSPITAL COURSE -
1) GI:  The patient was transferred from outside hospital with
bright red blood per rectum.  He had an NG lavage at the
outside hospital which was negative for any active bleeding.
Because of the repeated episodes of bleeding, GI elected to
perform a colonoscopy to assess if any intervention might be
possible to reduce risk of further bleeding.  This was performed
on [**8-28**] and showed diverticulosis but no active bleeding.
Because of his cardiovascular staus, the patient received no
sedation, and he tolerated the procedure well.  It was presumed
that he had bled from a diverticulum, and he had no further
episodes of rectal bleeding following his arrival at [**Hospital1 18**].
During the hospitalization, he received a total of 2 units of
blood to maintain a hematocrit greater than 30.

2) CARDIOVASCULAR - A) ISCHEMIA:  At the time of admission, the
patient had complaints of mild indigestion which were concerning
for possible angina.  He was initially ruled out for MI on
[**8-27**] with serial enzymes and EKG's.  The patient then
developed an episode of increased chest pain on the morning of
[**8-28**].  His EKG showed ST depression in leads V3 through V6,
consistent with a possible strain pattern.  Cardiac enzymes were
cycled with his initial set of enzymes negative. The patient
ruled-in with second set of enzymes with a peak CK of 2,822, with
an MB of 312, and a troponin of 4.4.  The patient was diagnosed
with a non-ST elevation MI in a setting of a GI bleed and
coronary artery disease.  Initially, he was managed medically
and transfused to maintain hematocrits greater than 30.
Cardiology was consulted to see the patient.

B) ARRHYTHMIA:  On the day following admission, [**8-28**], the
patient had a V-fib arrest at approximately 4:30 pm.  The
patient was found by physician to be pulseless.  A code was
called and CPR was initiated.  The patient's initial rhythm
was V-fib.  He received 3 shocks.  He then went into a PEA
rhythm and received both atropine and epinephrine.  The
patient also was given bicarb, along with IV fluids.  The
patient then converted into a rhythm of SVT with a rate of
150 and systolic blood pressure of 80.  His rhythm was
thought to be atrial fibrillation. The cardiologists concluded
the arrest was likely due to ischemia and that an emergent
cardiac catheterization with possible intervention would offer
the greatest chance of survival, and the family consented to the
procedure. He went to emergent cardiac catheterization which did
show two of his grafts were completely occluded, and he had a 90%
lesion in his SVG-OM graft which collateralized his LAD and RCA.
His SVG-OM graft was stented with an Express stent.  Stenting was
complicated by perforation which was quickly corrected without
any adverse consequences.  The patient was initially placed on
Integrilin drip.  However, this was held following his
perforation.  He was also started on aspirin and Plavix,
which were continued postcatheterization.  He was also
continued on a statin.  Beta blocker was held in the setting
of cardiogenic shock.  Following catheterization, the patient was
monitored closely on telemetry in the CCU.  He had no further
episodes of V-fib or V- tach.


C) PUMP:  After the arrest, the patient remained in severe
cardiogenic shock.  He was started on a dopamine drip, and
subsequently Levophed was added.  During the emergent cardiac
catheterization, an intra-aortic balloon pump was
placed for cardiogenic shock.  He was also continued on
Levophed and dopamine drips for pressure support.  Following
catheterization, the patient was slowly weaned off his
Levophed drip, and then off the dopamine drip.  The patient
had an elevated wedge pressure.  A Nipride drip was started
for afterload reduction, and he was slowly converted over to
po captopril and weaned off his Nipride drip.  The patient
was maintained on the intra-aortic balloon pump at a rate of
1:1.  His blood pressure did not tolerate any weaning off of
the balloon pump.

On [**8-31**], the patient had several hypotensive episodes.
He was restarted on the dopamine drip.  His hypotension was
thought to be a combination of cardiogenic shock, neurological
decompensation, and administration of sedating and vasodilatory
medications.

3) NEUROLOGIC:  The patient initially had no neurological
issues at time of admission.  Following his V-fib arrest, the
patient was unresponsive with a neurological exam concerning
for anoxic brain injury.  A CT of the head showed no gross
hemorrhage or edema.  It was significant only for old lacunar
infarcts in the basal ganglia.

Neurology was consulted for further evaluation.  An EEG was
obtained which showed epileptiform activity.  It also showed
moderate to moderately severe diffuse encephalopathy
consistent with anoxic brain injury.  The patient was thought
to be in status epilepticus and was initially loaded with
both ativan and Dilantin.  He had a slight decrease in his
epileptiform activity with this regimen.  Subsequently,
valproic acid was added.  The patient continued to have
seizure activity and was also started on phenobarbital.  The
patient did have cessation of his status epilepticus on this
multiple antiepileptic medication regimen.  A repeat EEG was
suggestive of severe generalized cerebral injury.

Given the patient's significant hypoxic brain injury
following prolonged V-fib arrest, in conjunction with his
status epilepticus and EEG findings, the patient's prognosis
was thought to be extremely poor.  The patient's severe
ischemic brain injury and extremely poor prognosis were
conveyed to the patient's family.  It was thought that the
patient had no meaningful chance of recovery, and based on
patient's previously expressed wishes, it was thought that he
would not desire continued supportive care, given his
neurologic injuries.

4) PULMONARY:  The patient was intubated at the time of his
V-fib arrest.  He was continued on the ventilator following
his transfer to the CCU.  He was briefly tried on pressure
support, but became apneic, and was then maintained on assist
control ventilation.

5) ID:  The patient initially had no ID issues upon
admission.  Following his V-fib arrest and transfer to the
unit, he did have significant leukocytosis.  This was thought
to be likely a stress response in conjunction with his
hypoxia.  The day following intubation, the patient began to
have increased secretions and was thought to have a likely
aspiration pneumonia.  His sputum culture showed rare
gram-negative rods and moderate growth of Staph aureus.  He
was started on Zosyn for antibiotic coverage for a presumed
aspiration pneumonia.  Blood cultures were also obtained
which showed no evidence of bacteremia.

6) FLUID, ELECTROLYTES AND NUTRITION:  The patient initially
kept NPO in preparation for colonoscopy, given his GI
bleeding.  He was then started on a cardiac "Heart Healthy
Diet."  His electrolytes were followed and repleted as needed
throughout the hospitalization.  The patient had significant
lactic acidosis following his V-fib arrest thought to be due
to his hypoxia.  His lactate was followed and trended down
without any further intervention.  He did receive bicarbonate
at the time of the code.  His electrolytes continued to be
followed closely while in the CCU.

7) ENDOCRINE:  The patient admitted with a history of type 2
diabetes and was initially placed on Glucophage per his home
regimen.  Following his admission to the unit, his Glucophage
was held, and he was instead placed on an Insulin drip.
However, his blood sugars remained normal, and the Insulin
drip was discontinued.  He maintained normoglycemia without
any active intervention.

8) PROPHYLAXIS:  He was placed on a proton pump inhibitor
for GI prophylaxis, given his GI bleed and his placement on
the ventilator.  He was also on a heparin drip for DVT
prophylaxis, given his intra-aortic balloon pump.

DISPOSITION:  Following patient's V-fib arrest with anoxic
brain injury, he remained unresponsive.  He was evaluated by
neurology.  Given his extremely poor prognosis, and patient's
wishes were discussed with the family, it was thought that
the patient would not wish to have continued supportive care,
given his current medical condition.  The patient's code
status was then changed to comfort measures only.  He was
started on a morphine drip, and his medications were
withdrawn, and the patient was extubated.  The patient
continued to be unresponsive, and his blood pressure and
heart rate trended down, and he became apneic.  The patient
then expired at 7:55 pm.  His family was notified of his
status.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES:
1. Lower gastrointestinal bleed secondary to diverticulosis.
2. Anemia.
3. Ventricular fibrillation arrest.
4. Coronary artery disease, status post cardiac
catheterization with stenting of saphenous vein graft-obtuse
marginal graft.
5. Anoxic brain injury.
6. Status epilepticus.
7. Cardiogenic shock.
8. Respiratory failure.
9. Aspiration pneumonia.
10.Lactic acidosis.
